name: aeronet
workload: wrk-driven HTTP/1.1 benchmark (1 thread, 30s duration, 5s warmup) across headers/body/body-codec/static/cpu/mixed/files/routing scenarios at 10 and 100 connections, run in CI against scripted competitor servers built from the same harness.
claimed_speedup: vs beast (10 conns): headers 12,035.73 vs 4,376.77 req/s (2.75x), static 54,259.34 vs 49,281.00 (1.10x), routing 57,644.49 vs 47,995.38 (1.20x). vs go net/http (10 conns): headers 12,035.73 vs 3,996.83 (3.0x), static 54,259.34 vs 25,399.27 (2.14x), routing 57,644.49 vs 28,141.20 (2.05x), mixed 25,261.40 vs 9,003.95 (2.81x), body 3,827.02 vs 407.32 (9.4x); at 100 conns aeronet leads go net/http in every scenario (e.g. static 93,479.14 vs 37,787.70, routing 91,957.05 vs 44,446.00) (all derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build on GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest (default GCC/Clang optimization, no explicit -O flags or compiler version pinned in CMakeLists.txt); Go server built with `go build` from go_server.go using stdlib net/http; Beast server (beast_server.cpp) built with Boost.Asio/Boost.Beast, same Release CMake config
tradeoffs: Linux-focused for peak performance (also supports macOS/Windows); benchmark harness builds and runs competitor servers (drogon, pistache, crow, beast, Rust Axum, Java Undertow, Go net/http, Python) itself in CI rather than using each project's own tuned deployment configuration, so absolute numbers may not reflect each competitor's best-case tuning.
caveats: First-party CI benchmark (project builds and runs all competitors itself); GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner is a generic shared/virtualized 2-vCPU host, not a named CPU model, and no compiler name/version is pinned, so this falls short of Tier A despite public benchmark code, full wrk parameters, and a live daily-updated dashboard. Numbers fluctuate run-to-run on shared CI hardware.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/TechEmpower/FrameworkBenchmarks/contents/frameworks/C++ (listed 'aeronet' as a tracked framework not on KNOWN_LIST), then gh search repos "aeronet" located sjanel/aeronet; confirmed via WebFetch on https://sjanel.github.io/aeronet/benchmarks/

name: uhttp (io_uring-http-benchmark)
workload: Serving a single 10,240-byte static HTML file over loopback on 2 physical cores; wrk from 6 separate client cores, 45s runs x3 repetitions, interleaved targets, at 64/256/1024/4096 connections, plus perf-measured instructions/cycles/IPC per request.
claimed_speedup: 40-54% more requests/sec than tuned nginx at the same connection counts (64 conns: 358,428 vs 256,046 req/s = +40%; 1024 conns: 315,095 vs 204,644 = +54%; 4096 conns: 276,195 vs 184,395 = +50%); 28-34% less CPU per request (5.8-7.5us vs nginx's 8.1-11.1us); half the instructions per request (17,583 vs 35,831) (verbatim from README table)
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build via liburing; compiler name/version not stated in repo (CMakeLists.txt has no explicit -O flags beyond default Release)
hardware: Unspecified 'mobile CPU', 2 physical cores each for server and 6 client cores; exact CPU model not stated; kernel built with CONFIG_INIT_ON_ALLOC_DEFAULT_ON=y
tradeoffs: Serves exactly one static route from memory (not general-purpose like nginx); no TLS/HTTP2/CGI; loopback-only benchmark so sendfile's zero-copy advantage on real NICs was not tested; author explicitly documents nginx wins the p99 latency tail at low connection counts and that per-feature attribution of the io_uring gains is unresolved.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (usability=reference despite public code). Exact CPU model and compiler are not stated (only 'mobile CPU' and CMake Release), so this is capped at Tier C per the first-party-benchmark rule even though methodology (warmup, repetitions, interleaving, perf counters) is unusually rigorous for a first-party repo. Author states loopback numbers should not be read as 'io_uring beats sendfile on a real network.'

name: epoll-httpd
workload: Static file serving over wrk (50 connections, 10s, server/client pinned to separate cores) for /index.html, 1KB, 8KB, and 64KB files, with nginx configured to match ehttpd's feature set (sendfile, keep-alive, open-file cache, no logging/gzip).
claimed_speedup: ~1.6x nginx headline (1KB file: 152,931 vs 96,792 req/s = 1.58x; index.html: 151,453 vs 82,510 = 1.84x; 8KB: 123,950 vs 89,014 = 1.39x; 64KB: parity at 0.94x); resident memory 4.1-5.2MB vs nginx's 10.4-10.5MB; across 4 repeated runs the 1KB ratio held 1.51x-1.67x and 8KB held 1.36x-1.42x (verbatim from README table, with author-documented run-to-run variance)
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release, CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE="-O2 -DNDEBUG" (from CMakeLists.txt); compiler name/version (gcc vs clang) not pinned or stated
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, 2 cores, Linux 6.18 (exact Xeon SKU not stated)
tradeoffs: Static-file-only server: no TLS, no HTTP/2, no chunked request bodies, no CGI/reverse proxying, no compression, no virtual hosts, IPv4 only, Linux-only (epoll/sendfile/timerfd/eventfd/accept4). At 64KB payloads it reaches parity with nginx once the kernel's sendfile copy path dominates, so the win is specific to small-payload per-request overhead.
caveats: First-party benchmark (project's own bench/run.sh), so capped at Tier C despite disclosing CPU frequency, core count, kernel version, and multi-run variance; exact CPU model/SKU and compiler name/version are not stated. Author flags the /index.html row as the least stable measurement (1.55x-2.90x across runs) because it is measured first in the loop before nginx settles.
